Can you repeat things we have done in class and on homework with limited access to resources? - Are you learning how to answer questions with data quickly? - Are you developing proficiency with R? ::: ::::: . . . ### Revision is a key part of this course design! # Portfolio Project 2 {.maize} # Regular Expressions (regex) {.maize} ## Regular expressions - Sometimes the patterns we wish to detect, extract, etc. too complex for exact matching + Extract all time stamps of the form `HH:MM:SS` + Extract the string that comes after the dash (e.g. `hw01-aluby`) - **Regular expressions** (regexps) are a very terse language that allow you to describe patterns in strings - Confusing at first, but extremely useful ## Example Suppose we wish to anonymize phone numbers in survey results ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} a1 <- "Home: 507-645-5489" a2 <- "Cell: 219.917.9871" a3 <- "My work phone is 507-202-2332" a4 <- "I don't have a phone" info <- c(a1, a2, a3, a4) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Home: 507-645-5489" "Cell: 219.917.9871" [3] "My work phone is 507-202-2332" "I don't have a phone" ``` ::: ::: ## Visualizing matches The helper function `str_view()` finds regex matches ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str_view(a1, "5") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] │ Home: <5>07-64<5>-<5>489 ``` ::: ::: ## `.` match any character Find a "-" and any (.) character that follows ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str_view(a1, "-.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] │ Home: 507<-6>45<-5>489 ``` ::: ::: ## `[]` match any occurence Find any numbers between 0 and 9 ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str_view(a1, "[0123456789]") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] │ Home: <5><0><7>-<6><4><5>-<5><4><8><9> ``` ::: ::: ## `[]` match any occurence Find any numbers between 2 and 7 ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str_view(a1, "[2-7]") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] │ Home: <5>0<7>-<6><4><5>-<5><4>89 ``` ::: ::: ## Your turn: ::: task Detect either "." or "-" in the `info` vector. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} a1 <- "Home: 507-645-5489" a2 <- "Cell: 219.917.9871" a3 <- "My work phone is 507-202-2332" a4 <- "I don't have a phone" info <- c(a1, a2, a3, a4) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Special patterns There are a number of special patterns that match more than one character ::: nonincremental - `\\d` - digit - `\\s` - white space - `\\w` - word - `\\t` - tab - `\\n` - newline ::: . . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str_view(a1, "\\d") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] │ Home: <5><0><7>-<6><4><5>-<5><4><8><9> ``` ::: ::: ::: aside Outside of R, these would be single back slashes. ::: ## Caution! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str_view(a1, "\\w") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] │ : <5><0><7>-<6><4><5>-<5><4><8><9> ``` ::: ::: ## `[^]` match any occurence except ANYTHING BUT numbers between 2 and 7 ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str_view(a1, "[^2-7]") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] │ <:>< >5<0>7<->645<->54<8><9> ``` ::: ::: ::: aside Common pitfall: forgetting the brackets ::: ## Anchors Anchors look for matches at the start `^` or end `$` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] │ Home: 507-645-5489 [2] │ Cell: 219.917.9871 [3] │ My work phone is 507-202-2332 [4] │ I don't have a phone ``` ::: ::: ::: panel-tabset ### Entries that start with a digit ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str_view(info, "^\\d") ``` ::: ### Entries that end with a digit ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str_view(info, "\\d$") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] │ Home: 507-645-548<9> [2] │ Cell: 219.917.987<1> [3] │ My work phone is 507-202-233<2> ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Use regex in `str_detect`, `str_sub`, etc: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str_view(info) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] │ Home: 507-645-5489 [2] │ Cell: 219.917.9871 [3] │ My work phone is 507-202-2332 [4] │ I don't have a phone ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str_detect(info, "\\d") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE TRUE TRUE FALSE ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str_replace_all(info, "\\d", "X") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Home: XXX-XXX-XXXX" "Cell: XXX.XXX.XXXX" [3] "My work phone is XXX-XXX-XXXX" "I don't have a phone" ``` ::: ::: ## Your turn ::: task A vector called `words` is loaded with `stringr` and contains a corpus of 980 words used in text analysis. Use `stringr` functions and regular expressions to find the words that satisfy the following descriptions. #### 1. Find all words that start with `y`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pattern <- "type your pattern here" str_subset(words, pattern) ``` ::: #### 2. Find all words that end with `x`. #### 3. Find all words that start with a vowel. #### 4. Find all words that start with consonants. ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Alternative patterns `|` allows you to match one or more alternative patterns ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str_view(info, "^H|C") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] │ ome: 507-645-5489 [2] │ ell: 219.917.9871 ``` ::: ::: ## "Fixing" the order of operations Why are these different? ::::: columns ::: {.column .nonincremental width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str_view(info, "^H|C.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] │ ome: 507-645-5489 [2] │ ll: 219.917.9871 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column .nonincremental width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str_view(info, "^(H|C).") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] │ me: 507-645-5489 [2] │ ll: 219.917.9871 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::::: ## Repetition You can search for a pattern followed by the number of matches ::::: columns ::: {.column .nonincremental width="50%"} - `?`: 0 or 1 - `+`: 1 or more - `*`: 0 or more - `{n}`: exactly n times - `{n,}`: n or more times - `{,m}`: at most m times - `{n,m}`: between n and m times ::: ::: {.column .nonincremental .fragment width="50%"} Example: detect three digits in a row ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str_view(a1, "\\d{3}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] │ Home: <507>-<645>-<548>9 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::::: ## Your turn: ::: task #### Find all words that are exactly three letters long. #### Find all words that end with `ing` or `ise`. #### Find all words that have seven letters or more. #### Find all words that start with three consonants. ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Duplicating groups Use escaped numbers (`\\1`, `\\2`, etc) to repeat a group based on position Which numbers have the same 1st and 3rd digits? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} phone_numbers <- c("515 111 2244", "310 549 6892", "474 234 7548") str_view(phone_numbers, "(\\d)\\d\\1") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] │ <515> <111> 2244 [3] │ <474> 234 7548 ``` ::: ::: # Intro to Text Analysis {.maize} ## Text Analysis Up to this point, we've been thinking of string data as a column in our dataset: - Names - Phone numbers - Addresses - Course titles - etc. . . . which are all relatively short and structured. We can extract meaning from them using relatively simple functions and "know what we're looking for". ## {background-image="../img/coursera-data-sci.png"} ## Sometimes, text data is more unstructured Random (?) sample of 26,882 reviews of coursera courses ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} en_coursera_reviews <- read_csv("https://stat220-w26.github.io/data/en_coursera_sample.csv") en_coursera_reviews ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 26,882 × 5 CourseId Review Label cld2 review_id 1 nurture-market-strategies It would be better if the … 1 en 1 2 nand2tetris2 Superb course. Great prese… 5 en 2 3 schedule-projects Excellent course! 5 en 3 4 teaching-english-capstone-2 I'd recommend this course … 5 en 4 5 machine-learning This course was so effecti… 5 en 5 6 python-network-data Words cannot describe how … 5 en 6 7 clinical-trials Great course! 5 en 7 8 python-genomics I didn't know anything abo… 3 en 8 9 strategic-management Loved everything about thi… 5 en 9 10 script-writing No significant instruction… 1 en 10 # ℹ 26,872 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: aside Source: [Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/septa97/100k-courseras-course-reviews-dataset/data) ::: *Note:* may need to install `tidytext` and `stopwords` packages ## Sometimes, text data is more unstructured ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} en_coursera_reviews %>% filter(str_detect(Review, "ggplot")) %>% pull(Review) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "So first of all, the material for this course in the bookdown document are very good - well structured, with good sources. My concern is that the Coursera course does not go a lot beyond, basically just referring to the document and adding quizzes + graded assignment in the last week. The assignment, however, is nice and challenging and requires people to understand the materials.Also, the course covers other great packages than ggplot2, e.g. plotly and leaflet and methods for handling spatial data. I think it would be very nice if the students were challenged in these topics as well and evaluate them in a better way than just a quiz (programming assignment for instance).I liked the course though and I believe it can be prepared even better." [3] "Good Intro to R.Basics of ggplot2 should have been covered along with base graphs or as a separate unit" [4] "Interesting, information-dense and well presented lectures by someone who obviously has a deep understanding of the topics and who is passionate about teaching the subject. Added to that: a great course textbook and useful R tutorials with a focus on commonly used libraries such as dplyr and ggplot. Beginner and intermediate statistics students, as well as teachers interested in the presentation of statistics theory and practice, can't go wrong with this course." [5] "ggplot2 module was extremely helpful" [6] "This course provides a great overiew to introductory R programming. Since taking the course, I have successfully used the precepts learned here for a number of analysis projects. Coupled with ggplot2 graphics, the results became self-evident." [7] "Lecture videos were fantastic! Instructor was amazing. I have a big problem with the final project in Week 5. The entire courses was focused on statistics, yet the final project was focused on R. I wish I had prior R knowledge before starting this course, yet on the front page it says it's a beginner specialization. I would recommend learning R and ggplot before this course. It will make the course a lot less frustrating!" [8] "Overall, I would recommend this class. I found that the preparation towards the final project could use some improvement, especially plotting using the 'ggplot2' package. Also, I found that the project was a little bit too open-ended and could have used some more input from the instructors' side. The material during the four weeks of the course was really good and thorough but perhaps a little too difficult to follow for people who have absolutely no background in probability theory. Maybe one should audit the course first and then decide whether it would be a good idea to formally enroll." ``` ::: ::: ## {.center} ::::: columns ::: {.column .nonincremental width="50%"} ![](https://juliasilge.github.io/tidytext/reference/figures/tidytext.png){width="60%"} ::: :::{.column .nonincremental width="50%"} - Functions for text analysis that follow tidy data principles - *Not* part of the `tidyverse`, but plays well with other packages ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidytext) ``` ::: ::: ::::: ## Some notation *document*: an observation of text data (in this case, an abstract) . . . *corpus*: collection of many documents . . . *token*: a unit of analysis within the document (typically a word, but could be a sentence or a line or a pair of words, etc.) ## Text as tidy data 1. *tokenize* each document - Each *row* in the dataset is a token 2. Remove *stopwords* - Words like "the" and "is" typically aren't interesting - Makes the dataset smaller and easier to work with 3. Count the tokens 4. (optional) *fancy count* the tokens - Standardize based on total number of tokens - How common is a token *relative to other documents* - How common are "good words" or "bad words" ## `unnest_tokens()` ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} - `tbl`: our data - `output`: what should the output column be called? - `input`: what column do we tokenize? - `token`: default is "word" but can also be "ngrams", "sentences", "lines", "paragraphs", etc. - `to_lower`: should tokens be converted to lowercase ::: ::: {.column .nonincremental width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} unnest_tokens( tbl, output, input, token = "words", to_lower = TRUE, drop = TRUE, ... ) ``` ::: ::: ::::: ## Tokenize ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidytext) en_coursera_reviews |> unnest_tokens(output = word, input = Review) |> select(CourseId, word) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 666,493 × 2 CourseId word 1 nurture-market-strategies it 2 nurture-market-strategies would 3 nurture-market-strategies be 4 nurture-market-strategies better 5 nurture-market-strategies if 6 nurture-market-strategies the 7 nurture-market-strategies instructors 8 nurture-market-strategies cared 9 nurture-market-strategies to 10 nurture-market-strategies respond # ℹ 666,483 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Make it ~ fancy ~: tf-idf Idea: how common are certain tokens *relative to the rest of the documents in the corpus*? . . . tf(t,d) = "term frequency": what proportion of document d is term t? . . . idf = "inverse document frequency": log-scaled inverse fraction of documents that contain the term $$\text{idf} = \log \frac{\text{number of documents}}{\text{number of documents containing term t}}$$ . . . $$\text{tf-df(t, d)} = \frac{\text{tf(t, d)}}{\text{idf(t)}}$$ ## highest tf-idf's are used a lot within a review, and rarely in other reviews ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} en_coursera_reviews |> left_join(coursera_reviews, by = c("review_id")) |> unnest_tokens(word, review_clean) |> count(review_id, word) |> bind_tf_idf(word, review_id, n) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 211,280 × 6 review_id word n tf idf tf_idf 1 1 cared 1 0.25 8.81 2.20 2 1 instructors 1 0.25 4.43 1.11 3 1 queries 1 0.25 7.80 1.95 4 1 respond 1 0.25 8.00 2.00 5 2 challenging 1 0.0833 4.02 0.335 6 2 developers 1 0.0833 6.98 0.582 7 2 fun 1 0.0833 3.73 0.311 8 2 highly 1 0.0833 3.56 0.297 9 2 levels 1 0.0833 6.67 0.556 10 2 material 1 0.0833 3.09 0.257 # ℹ 211,270 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## highest tf-idf's are used a lot within a review, and rarely in other reviews ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} en_coursera_reviews |> unnest_tokens(word, Review) |> count(review_id, word) |> bind_tf_idf(word, review_id, n) |> group_by(word) |> mutate(total_n = sum(n)) |> ungroup() |> arrange(desc(tf_idf)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 547,524 × 7 review_id word n tf idf tf_idf total_n 1 3970 excellen 1 1 10.2 10.2 1 2 5501 estupendo 1 1 10.2 10.2 1 3 25198 excellant 1 1 9.51 9.51 2 4 10057 impeccable 1 1 9.10 9.10 3 5 13780 satisfactory 1 1 8.59 8.59 5 6 26553 magnificent 1 1 8.12 8.12 8 7 7751 excellence 1 1 7.90 7.90 10 8 10971 excellence 1 1 7.90 7.90 10 9 12755 recomendable 1 1 7.90 7.90 10 10 13077 excellence 1 1 7.90 7.90 10 # ℹ 547,514 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="4|5-6|7,10"} en_coursera_reviews |> unnest_tokens(word, Review) |> count(CourseId, review_id, word) |> bind_tf_idf(word, review_id, n) |> filter(str_detect(CourseId, "data-science")) |> group_by(CourseId) %>% slice_max(tf_idf, n = 10) %>% ggplot(aes(x = n, y = fct_reorder(word, n))) + geom_col() + facet_wrap(~CourseId, scales = "free_y", nrow = 2) + labs( y = "word" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](slides14_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-46-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ##
